snippet.title: What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
snippet.description:
Gliese 710 is an orange dwarf star heading towards the Solar System. In about 1.3 million years, its predicted journey through the distant Oort Cloud could reshape the comet traffic around the Sun — while staying far beyond the planets.

Follow the Gaia measurements, the scale of the flyby and the changing night sky, from a star we cannot see unaided today to a future bright orange visitor.

Chapters
0:00 A star on the move
0:42 The Star Heading Our Way
2:06 How Close Will It Come?
3:29 Into the Oort Cloud
4:41 The Comet Shower
5:35 A New Brightest Star
6:17 It Has Happened Before

Sources: Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a); Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — peak brightness and the predicted comet shower (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835); NASA Science, Oort Cloud Facts — the distant comet reservoir (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/); Mamajek et al. (2015), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 800 L17 — the past flyby of Scholz’s star (https://doi.org/10.1088/2041-8205/800/1/L17); Levison et al. (2010), Science 329, 187–190 — capture of comets in the Sun’s birth cluster (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1187535).

snippet.title: Why Will Gliese 710's Comets Arrive After It Has Gone?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

Gliese 710 is predicted to send about 10 extra comets a year into the inner Solar System for three to four million years — yet the comet shower peaks only after the star has already passed and is heading away again, because falling in from the distant Oort Cloud takes hundreds of thousands of years.

Sources: Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — predicted Oort Cloud comet flux (~10 observable comets/yr lasting 3–4 Myr) (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · NASA Science, Oort Cloud Facts — the distant comet reservoir (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/).

Pictures: NASA STS-83 Space Shuttle photograph of Comet Hale-Bopp over Earth's airglow limb, NASA ISS photograph of Comet C/2023 A3 Tsuchinshan-ATLAS by Matthew Dominick, and ESO La Silla Observatory night-sky star-trails time-lapse by R. Wesson (CC BY 4.0), alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/JSC; NASA/Matthew Dominick; R. Wesson/ESO (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

snippet.title: Is a Star Really Coming Towards Us?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

In the constellation Serpens, the orange dwarf star Gliese 710 is heading nearly straight towards our Solar System at about 51,000 kilometres an hour. In roughly 1.3 million years, it will sail right through the outer edge of the Solar System — the icy shell of the Oort Cloud.

Sources: Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance, velocity, and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — Gliese 710 flyby and Oort Cloud encounter (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · NASA Science, Oort Cloud Facts — the distant comet reservoir (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/).

Pictures: ESA/Gaia/DPAC proper-motion starfield sweep across 1.6 million years and ESA/Gaia/DPAC EDR3 all-sky Milky Way star map (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO), alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: ESA/Gaia/DPAC (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/igo/).

snippet.title: How Close Will Gliese 710 Come to the Sun?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

Gaia measurements put Gliese 710's closest approach at about a fifth of a light-year — roughly 13,000 times the Earth–Sun distance. If the gap between the Sun and Earth were one centimetre, Neptune would sit 30 centimetres away on a ruler, and Gliese 710 would pass more than 100 metres away, the length of a football pitch.

Sources: Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 closest-approach distance of 10,635–16,649 AU (~0.21 light-years) (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — Gliese 710 encounter and Oort Cloud scale (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835).

Pictures: NASA/JPL Voyager 2 full-disk photograph of Neptune (PIA01492), alongside original animated explainers, AI-generated scenes, and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/JPL.

snippet.title: What Will the Night Sky Look Like When Gliese 710 Arrives?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

At closest approach in about 1.3 million years, the orange dwarf Gliese 710 will become the brightest star in the night sky — about three times brighter than Sirius, as bright as Jupiter at its best — and creep across the sky by the width of the full Moon every 35 years.

Sources: Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — peak brightness at magnitude −2.7 (about 3× brighter than Sirius) and perihelion proper motion of 52.28″/yr (~1 full-Moon width every 35.6 years) (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a).

Pictures: ESO La Silla night-sky and star-trails time-lapses by S. Brunier and R. Wesson (CC BY 4.0), NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA WISE infrared sky photograph, NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS Juno colour-enhanced photograph of Jupiter (PIA21974), and NASA/GSFC/ASU Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter full-Moon photograph, alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: ESO/S. Brunier; R. Wesson/ESO; NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA; NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS; NASA/GSFC/ASU.

snippet.title: What Happens When Gliese 710 Passes Through the Oort Cloud?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

Sunlight reaches Earth in about eight minutes, yet it would take months to travel out to the distant Oort Cloud where the orange dwarf Gliese 710 is heading. When the star passes through in about 1.3 million years, its gravity will brush through that vast cloud of icy bodies and nudge the comets nearest its path.

Sources: Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — Gliese 710 trajectory through the Oort Cloud and comet perturbation (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · NASA Science, Oort Cloud Facts — the distant comet reservoir (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/).

Pictures: NASA GSFC Solar Dynamics Observatory solar-flare eruption video, ESA/Gaia/DPAC proper-motion starfield animation (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO), NASA photograph of Comet NEOWISE over Washington, D.C. by Bill Ingalls, ESO La Silla New Technology Telescope night-sky time-lapse (CC BY 4.0), and NASA STS-83 Space Shuttle photograph of Comet Hale-Bopp, alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/SDO; ESA/Gaia/DPAC (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/igo/); NASA/Bill Ingalls; ESO (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); NASA/JSC.
